8961.heading: Linguistic Proximity Analysis
8961.content:
Linguistic proximity analysis measures how closely marker sets occur within text to investigate their semantic relationship. A narrow token window suggests tight coupling, while a wide window may capture separate discussions that merely share a page or document.

The chosen distance changes the number and interpretation of returns. Proximity is therefore a methodological assumption that must be justified and tested rather than an arbitrary search setting.

8964.content:
A linguistic marker set is an explicitly developed group of words or forms used to represent a concept in a text corpus. It replaces a single intuitive keyword with a set grounded in how the corpus actually expresses the idea.

Marker construction is iterative. Researchers explore language use, add or remove forms, and examine associations so the set captures meaningful variation without admitting excessive false positives.

8967.title: Linguistic Boundary
8967.heading: Linguistic Boundary
8967.content: A linguistic boundary appears where a term's meaning changes between business capabilities. “Product” can refer to marketing content, inventory stock, purchasing terms, or warehouse handling, each with different properties and behavior. Treating those meanings as one object causes ambiguity and unrelated change. Identifying the boundary is a strong first method for finding a [[Bounded Context]] because it shows where one [[Ubiquitous Language]] stops being precise and another must begin.

8970.title: Linguistic Aggregation
8970.heading: Linguistic Aggregation
8970.content:
Linguistic aggregation combines related pieces of information into a more compact utterance. Instead of repeating a full sentence for every result, a generator can coordinate facts, group shared properties, or summarize a list.

Aggregation improves efficiency but requires attention to clarity and cognitive load. The [[Sentence Planner]] must decide which details can be combined without obscuring distinctions the user needs.

8976.title: Linearly Separable Data
8976.heading: Linearly Separable Data
8976.content:
Linearly separable data can be divided into classes by a linear [[Decision Boundary]]. In two dimensions the boundary is a straight line, in three dimensions it is a plane, and in higher dimensions it generalizes to a hyperplane.

A single artificial neuron using a step activation can learn this kind of separation. Concentric or otherwise nonlinear class regions require an [[Artificial Neural Network]] that combines several neurons and hidden layers.

8979.title: Linearity Assumption
8979.heading: Linearity Assumption
8979.content:
The linearity assumption states that the expected continuous outcome is an additive linear function of the predictors as represented in the model. It concerns the mean structure, not whether each raw variable has a normal distribution.

Residual patterns and scatter plots can expose curvature or thresholds. Transformations, splines, interactions, or categorical representations may address departures, but each alternative changes what the coefficients mean.

8981.heading: Document

8982.sourceSearchName: linear time prefix clustering linear time prefix clustering
8982.title: Linear-Time Prefix Clustering
8982.heading: Linear-Time Prefix Clustering
8982.content:
Prefix clustering assigns each encoded record to the branches determined by its successive digits. The book argues that a Baire hierarchy can be read in one scan of the input rather than constructed from all pairs of observations, which ordinary agglomerative clustering often requires.

The linear-time claim applies to the scan when code length or measurement precision is treated as bounded. A useful comparison must still account for the cost of creating codes, random projections for multidimensional data, storage, and any later refinement of coarse bins. Speed does not guarantee the bins reflect the intended domain similarity.

8983.heading: References

8985.title: Linear Velocity
8985.heading: Linear Velocity
8985.content: Linear velocity is the rate of change of [[Displacement]]. Average velocity is $\Delta s/\Delta t$, while instantaneous velocity is $v=ds/dt$. Because it is a vector, a change in direction is a velocity change even if speed remains constant. The gradient of a velocity-time graph is [[Acceleration]].

8987.title: Linear Time Complexity

8988.sourceSearchName: linear time complexity linear time complexity
8988.title: Linear Time Complexity
8988.heading: Linear Time Complexity
8988.content:
Linear time complexity, written $O(n)$, means that the work performed grows in direct proportion to [[Input Size]]. Doubling the number of items therefore multiplies the leading amount of work by approximately two.

[[Linear Search]] has linear worst-case time because it may need to inspect every item. Linear behavior is often the best possible when an [[Algorithm]] must read all $n$ input elements at least once.

8991.title: Linear System
8991.heading: Linear System
8991.content:
A linear system is a collection of linear equations in common unknowns. It can be written compactly as $Ax=b$, using a [[Coefficient Matrix]] $A$, an unknown vector $x$, and a right-hand-side vector $b$.

Depending on rank and dimensions, a system may have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions. Numerical methods exploit matrix structure to solve it efficiently and accurately.

The source introduces matrix algebra through simultaneous scalar equations and then returns to the same structure when solving least-squares normal equations. Whether the coefficient matrix has independent columns determines whether the fitted parameter vector is uniquely identifiable.

8994.sourceSearchName: linear strain triangle linear strain triangle
8994.title: Linear Strain Triangle
8994.heading: Linear Strain Triangle
8994.content:
A linear strain triangle is a higher-order triangular structural element whose displacement interpolation permits strain to vary linearly within the element. Midside nodes provide more degrees of freedom than a constant strain triangle.

It can represent curved boundaries and changing stress fields more accurately with fewer elements. The additional nodes enlarge the element matrix and computational work.

8997.title: Linear Separability
8997.heading: Linear Separability
8997.content:
Linear separability means that classes can be divided without error by a line, plane, or higher-dimensional hyperplane. A single perceptron learning rule is guaranteed to find such a boundary when one exists under its assumptions.

Problems such as exclusive-or are not linearly separable. They require a representation or model with nonlinear capacity, such as a multilayer network.

9000.title: Linear Search
9000.heading: Linear Search
9000.content:
Linear search examines items one at a time until it finds the target or exhausts the collection. It is also called sequential search.

For an unordered collection of $n$ items, the target could be last or absent, so the worst-case [[Time Complexity]] is $O(n)$. On a [[Linked List]], the algorithm begins at the head and follows each [[Pointer]] to the next node until it finds a match or reaches null.

9003.title: Linear Regression Intercept
9003.heading: Linear Regression Intercept
9003.content:
The linear regression intercept is the model's predicted outcome when every numeric predictor equals zero and every indicator is in its reference state. It anchors the fitted equation from which other coefficients add or subtract.

The intercept may lack a practical interpretation when zero is outside the observed range or the combined reference profile is unrealistic. Centering predictors can give it a more meaningful reference without changing the fitted relationships.

For a two-group indicator design in the source, the intercept equals the fitted mean of the reference group. The indicator coefficient then adds the estimated difference needed to reach the second group mean.

9006.sourceSearchName: linear regression model presentation linear regression model presentation
9006.title: Linear Regression Model Presentation
9006.heading: Linear Regression Model Presentation
9006.content:
A linear regression model presentation organizes coefficient estimates and their uncertainty by substantive category and level. It commonly shows an unadjusted model, a partially adjusted model, and the fully adjusted final model so readers can see how adjustment changes the exposure estimate.

Reference groups and absent terms must be labeled explicitly. Exporting a tidy model table reduces transcription errors, while a [[Coefficient Plot]] can support interpretation of direction, magnitude, and precision.

9009.title: Linear Regression
9009.heading: Linear Regression
9009.content:
Linear regression models a continuous outcome as an intercept plus weighted contributions from one or more explanatory variables. Each coefficient describes the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit predictor change, holding the other modeled variables constant.

Valid interpretation depends on the variable coding, residual behavior, and study design. A statistically significant coefficient describes an adjusted association on the outcome scale; it does not by itself establish causation.

The source writes the full model as $Y=X\beta+\epsilon$, where the design matrix expresses the experimental comparison and least squares estimates the coefficient vector. This same formulation accommodates transformed predictors, several factors, and interaction terms without changing the core fitting principle.

9011.sourceSearchName: linear regression confidence interval linear regression confidence interval
9011.title: Linear Regression Confidence Interval
9011.heading: Document

9012.sourceSearchName: linear regression confidence interval linear regression confidence interval
9012.title: Linear Regression Confidence Interval
9012.heading: Linear Regression Confidence Interval
9012.content:
A linear regression confidence interval gives a range of coefficient values compatible with the data and model at a stated confidence level. It is formed from the estimate and its standard error under the fitted model's sampling assumptions.

An interval containing zero does not support a nonzero association at the corresponding two-sided significance level. Its width communicates precision more directly than a p-value and should be interpreted in the outcome's units.

9015.sourceSearchName: linear regression coefficient linear regression coefficient
9015.title: Linear Regression Coefficient
9015.heading: Linear Regression Coefficient
9015.content:
A linear regression coefficient is the estimated change in a continuous outcome associated with a one-unit increase in a predictor while the other model terms remain fixed. For an [[Indicator Variable]], it is the adjusted mean difference from the reference group.

Its sign gives direction and its magnitude remains in outcome units. The standard error, confidence interval, and p-value describe estimation uncertainty, while subject-matter context determines whether the change is important.

The source emphasizes that a coefficient's meaning follows from its design-matrix column. With an indicator, it may represent a group difference; with a continuous predictor, a slope; and with a product column, an interaction adjustment to another effect.

9018.heading: Linear Quadrilateral Element
9018.content:
A linear quadrilateral element is a four-node two-dimensional element used to cover planar domains. Each node carries in-plane translational degrees of freedom, and bilinear interpolation represents the displacement field.

Quadrilaterals can be efficient in regular regions but their accuracy deteriorates with excessive distortion. Mesh layout should align elements with geometry and important stress gradients when possible.

9021.title: Linear Programming
9021.heading: Linear Programming
9021.content:
Linear programming optimizes a linear objective subject to linear equality or inequality constraints. Decision variables usually also satisfy sign restrictions.

The feasible points form a polygon or higher-dimensional polyhedron, and an optimum, when it exists, can be found at an extreme point. The [[Simplex Method]] moves between basic feasible solutions.

9024.title: Linear Programming Sensitivity Analysis
9024.heading: Linear Programming Sensitivity Analysis
9024.content:
Linear programming sensitivity analysis studies how changes in objective coefficients, constraint coefficients, resource limits, variables, or constraints affect an optimal solution.

For right-hand-side changes that preserve the current basis, a shadow price gives the change in optimal objective value per additional unit of a resource. Larger changes may require reoptimization.

9027.title: Linear Programming Duality
9027.heading: Linear Programming Duality
9027.content:
Linear programming duality associates a second optimization problem with a primal program. Constraints in one correspond to variables in the other, and a maximization problem is paired with a minimization problem.

Weak duality bounds any primal feasible value by any dual feasible value. When optimal solutions exist, the primal and dual objective values are equal.

9030.heading: Linear Potential Element
9030.content:
A linear potential element interpolates scalar potential between element nodes with first-order shape functions. In one dimension, two endpoint values define a straight-line variation whose derivative is constant inside the element.

The interpolation functions sum to one and reproduce their own nodal value. Substitution into a variational, weighted-residual, or direct formulation produces the element coefficient matrix.

9033.title: Linear Objective Function
9033.heading: Linear Objective Function
9033.content:
A linear objective function has the form $c^Tx$, a weighted sum of the [[Decision Variable|decision variables]]. A linear program seeks to maximize or minimize this quantity.

The coefficients express the contribution of one unit of each variable, such as profit or cost. They do not alter the feasible region but determine which feasible extreme point is preferred.

9036.heading: Linear Level Layout
9036.content:
A linear level layout requires spaces to be experienced in a fixed sequence, with movement mainly to the next or previous area. The geometric shape need not be a straight line.

Linearity gives strong control over teaching, pacing, and story order but offers little route choice. One-way transitions can prevent backtracking, while excessive constraint can make the player feel carried through the level.

9039.title: Linear Momentum
9039.heading: Linear Momentum
9039.content: Linear momentum is the vector $p=mv$, the product of mass and velocity. Its SI unit is $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, equivalent to a newton-second. The total momentum of a system changes only through external impulse, making momentum especially useful for analyzing collisions, explosions, and propulsion.

9042.sourceSearchName: linear model assumption test linear model assumption test
9042.title: Linear Model Assumption Test
9042.heading: Linear Model Assumption Test
9042.content:
A linear model assumption test evaluates features such as skewness, kurtosis, link specification, and heteroscedasticity in a fitted model's residual behavior. A global test combines several diagnostics into one assessment.

With very large samples, small departures can yield extremely small p-values, so formal rejection should be interpreted with graphical evidence and the analysis goal. The test identifies inconsistency with assumptions; it does not automatically prescribe the best alternative model.

9045.heading: Linear Model Power Calculation
9045.content:
A linear model power calculation uses an effect-size measure for explained variance together with numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, significance level, and target power. It aligns planning more directly with regression than a two-group t-test approximation.

The numerator degrees of freedom reflect the tested predictors, while the solved denominator degrees of freedom imply the required residual information and sample size. Adding parameters without increasing effect can raise the required sample.

9048.title: Linear Least Squares
9048.heading: Linear Least Squares
9048.content:
Linear least squares fits a line $y=a+bx$ by minimizing the [[Residual Sum of Squares]]. Setting the derivatives with respect to $a$ and $b$ to zero produces two normal equations.

Although the fitted model is a line, the method generalizes directly to several linear parameters by writing the observations as $Ax\approx b$ and solving the [[Normal Equation]].

The source applies least squares to outcome vector $Y$ and design matrix $X$, choosing coefficients that minimize the residual sum of squares. This formulation covers group comparisons, continuous predictors, polynomial terms, and interactions within the same matrix framework.

9051.title: Linear Kernel Classifier
9051.heading: Linear Kernel Classifier
9051.content:
A linear kernel classifier uses the ordinary dot product between feature vectors. In an SVM, this produces a hyperplane directly in the original feature space.

The linear kernel is especially attractive for sparse, high-dimensional data because it avoids expensive nonlinear similarity calculations and yields a compact weight vector. Its limitation is representational: classes that require a curved boundary cannot be separated without changing the features.

9054.title: Linear Inequality
9054.heading: Linear Inequality
9054.content: A linear inequality compares a first-degree expression with another quantity. Addition or subtraction of the same value preserves its direction, as does multiplication by a positive value. Multiplication or division by a negative value reverses the inequality. Its solution is usually an interval rather than a single number.

9060.heading: Linear Inequality in One Variable
9060.content:
A linear inequality in one variable compares linear expressions whose unknown appears only to the first power. A typical form is

$$ax+b<c$$

or the corresponding (>), (\leq), or (\geq) relation.

Solving isolates the variable by applying compatible operations to both sides. Addition and subtraction preserve the relation, as does multiplication or division by a positive value. A negative multiplier requires [[Reversing an Inequality]]. The answer is a set of values rather than usually one number.

9063.title: Linear Independence
9063.heading: Linear Independence
9063.content:
Vectors are linearly independent when $c_1v_1+\cdots+c_nv_n=0$ implies that every coefficient is zero.

Independence means no vector in the set can be constructed from the others. A linearly independent spanning set forms a [[Basis]], and eigenvectors associated with distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.

9066.title: Linear Equation
9066.heading: Linear Equation
9066.content: A linear equation in one unknown can be written $ax+b=0$ with $a\ne0$. Its single solution is $x=-b/a$. Solving consists of reversible arithmetic steps that isolate the unknown, so maintaining [[Equivalent Equations]] at each step preserves the solution set.

9072.title: Linear Equation in One Variable
9072.heading: Linear Equation in One Variable
9072.content:
A linear equation in one variable can be written in the form

$$ax+b=c,$$

where (a\neq0) and (a), (b), and (c) are real numbers. The unknown appears only to the first power.

Solving reverses the operations surrounding the variable: subtract (b) from both sides and divide by (a), giving (x=(c-b)/a). More complicated-looking equations may become linear after distributing, combining like terms, or clearing denominators. [[Equation Verification]] checks the resulting value.

9075.title: Linear Dependence
9075.heading: Linear Dependence
9075.content:
Vectors are linearly dependent when some nontrivial [[Linear Combination]] equals the [[Zero Vector]]. Equivalently, at least one vector can be written as a combination of the others.

Adding more vectors to an already dependent set cannot restore independence. Dependence reveals redundant directions in a matrix or spanning set.

9078.title: Linear Constraint
9078.heading: Linear Constraint
9078.content:
A linear constraint restricts decision variables through a linear equality or inequality such as $a^Tx\leq b$.

Each inequality defines a half-space, and all constraints together define the set of [[Feasible Solution|feasible solutions]]. Slack, surplus, or artificial variables can convert constraints into equations for the [[Simplex Method]].

9081.title: Linear Combination
9081.heading: Linear Combination
9081.content:
A linear combination of vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is a weighted sum $c_1v_1+\cdots+c_nv_n$ using scalar coefficients.

All linear combinations of a set form its [[Span]]. Whether a combination can equal the zero vector with nonzero coefficients determines [[Linear Independence]].

A statistical model remains linear when the known predictor columns are combined with unknown scalar coefficients, even if a predictor itself contains a transformed quantity such as squared time. Linearity refers to the coefficient combination rather than the visual shape of the fitted curve.

9084.heading: Line Segment Plane Intersection
9084.content:
Line segment-plane intersection substitutes a segment's parametric equation into the plane equation and solves for the segment parameter. A value between zero and one places the hit between the two endpoints.

A negative value lies behind the start, and a value greater than one lies beyond the end. A near-zero denominator indicates that the segment direction is parallel or nearly parallel to the plane.

9087.content:
A line segment is the finite set of points between a start and an end. A parametric representation adds a fraction from zero to one of the end-minus-start vector to the start point.

Collision tests use that bounded parameter to reject intersections located behind the start or beyond the end. Segments support weapon traces, visibility checks, projectiles, and a [[Segment Cast]] against the physics world.

9093.heading: Limits to Growth
9093.content:
Limits to growth is a system pattern in which a [[Reinforcing Loop]] initially drives rapid expansion, but a limiting resource activates a [[Balancing Loop]]. Growth then slows into an S-shaped path or overshoots and crashes.

The pattern matters in progression and economy design because apparently stable growth can conceal a constraint that emerges only later. Recognizing the limiting stock or flow allows the designer to shape the transition intentionally.

9096.sourceSearchName: limits of responsible innovation limits of responsible innovation
9096.title: Limits of Responsible Innovation
9096.heading: Limits of Responsible Innovation
9096.content:
The limits of responsible innovation appear when ethical design methods assume that a proposed technology will be built and ask only how to make it acceptable. Under that assumption, ethics can become a lubricant for development or a public justification for business as usual.

Some applications may be too unreliable, harmful, or illegitimate to deploy. A genuine ethical process must preserve the option to pause, reject, or redirect a project. It must also acknowledge that values cannot always be fully articulated as design requirements and that consequences emerge through social use. [[Responsible Innovation]] is strongest when it retains this critical space.

9102.heading: Limits of Computational Problem Solving
9102.content:
Computational problems face two fundamental limits. Some have no algorithmic solution, while others have algorithms whose time or storage grows so rapidly that no available machine can finish them in a useful period.

Good computational thinking identifies these limits early and seeks alternatives such as [[Algorithmic Heuristic|heuristics]], approximation, changed representations, or a narrower problem. It also recognizes social and political questions that computation can illuminate but cannot settle.

9111.title: Likelihood
9111.heading: Likelihood
9111.content:
Likelihood evaluates how compatible observed data is with a proposed hypothesis or parameter value. Written as $P(data \mid hypothesis)$, it is viewed as a function of the hypothesis while the observed data remains fixed.

Likelihood weights prior alternatives during Bayesian inference and supplies the objective for maximum-likelihood estimation. It is not generally normalized across hypothesis values until combined with the other model factors.

For independent observations, the source multiplies their model probabilities to form a joint likelihood. Holding the observed counts fixed while varying a Poisson rate turns this expression into the function optimized by [[Maximum Likelihood Estimation]].

9114.title: Like Terms
9114.heading: Like Terms
9114.content:
Like terms have the same variable factors raised to the same corresponding powers. Their order can differ because multiplication is commutative, so (4a^2b^3) and (7b^3a^2) are like terms.

Only their [[Numerical Coefficient]]s may differ. Terms such as (4a) and (4a^2), or (4ab^2) and (4ab^3), are unlike because at least one exponent differs. Matching structure permits [[Combining Like Terms]]; superficial similarity in letters is not enough.

Lightmap Pack separates selected faces and arranges them as nonoverlapping UV islands. The layout is designed for baked information that requires each surface region to occupy its own unambiguous texture area.

9120.title: Light Probe
9120.heading: Light Probe
9120.content:
A light probe captures illumination arriving from many directions at a point in a real scene. A reflective sphere, calibrated camera arrangement, or related method can turn the observed light into an environment representation for virtual rendering.

The probe samples illumination at one place and time, so moving lights, outdoor change, and spatially varying conditions require new observations or a richer model. Its purpose is to make virtual shading and reflections agree with the environment.

Lexicographic order compares exponent vectors at the first coordinate where they differ. The monomial with the larger exponent at that position is ordered first.

Because earlier variables dominate every comparison, lexicographic order supports the [[Elimination Theorem]]. A Gröbner basis computed in this order exposes equations involving only later variables.

9141.title: Lexicalization
9141.heading: Lexicalization
9141.content:
Lexicalization selects the words and grammatical forms used to realize a planned meaning. It resolves choices such as vocabulary, agreement, number, and gender while preserving the intended content.

In a generation pipeline, lexicalization follows a [[Sentence Planner]] and [[Microplanner]]. Even template systems perform a limited form of lexicalization when they insert and format variable values.

9144.title: Lexical Analysis
9144.heading: Lexical Analysis
9144.content:
Lexical analysis reads a stream of source characters and groups them into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, operators, and keywords. Whitespace and comments are handled according to the language's rules rather than passed directly to later stages.

The token sequence gives [[Syntax Analysis]] a simpler symbolic input. Invalid characters or malformed literals can be reported with source locations during this first stage of a custom scripting language.

9147.title: Levenshtein Edit Distance
9147.heading: Levenshtein Edit Distance
9147.content:
Levenshtein edit distance is the minimum number of allowed single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform one string into another. It gives a direct measure of surface-form similarity between two character sequences.

The distance can rank dictionary replacements for misspellings and support approximate matching of messages or document fragments. It does not capture semantic equivalence: two differently worded statements can have high edit distance even when they mean the same thing.

9150.content:
A level file schema defines how global settings, actors, components, types, and properties are organized in persistent data. A predictable structure lets the loader validate expected arrays and objects before constructing runtime state.

The schema is a contract between authoring tools and the engine. Adding or renaming fields requires compatibility decisions so older content either receives defaults, migrates, or fails with a useful error.

9153.title: Level Design
9153.heading: Level Design
9153.content:
Level design arranges space, challenges, events, objects, resources, atmosphere, and pacing to produce a particular segment of player experience. It turns general game rules and world content into moment-to-moment play.

The work is cross-disciplinary. Layout must coordinate with story, art, audio, programming, core mechanics, and the actions the player has already learned.

9156.title: Level Atmosphere
9156.heading: Level Atmosphere
9156.content:
Level atmosphere is the mood created by the specific arrangement of environment art, lighting, sound, events, and pacing. The level designer assembles assets so they feel coherent with the game world and intended emotion.

Atmosphere should also support play. Visual and audio choices must preserve navigation, threat recognition, and important feedback instead of obscuring them for decoration.

9159.title: Lepton
9159.heading: Lepton
9159.content: A lepton is an elementary particle that does not participate in the strong interaction. The charged leptons are the electron, muon, and tau, each paired with a neutral neutrino; every lepton has a corresponding antiparticle. Lepton-family numbers and electric charge constrain allowed particle transformations.

9162.heading: Lenz's Law
9162.content: Lenz's law states that an induced current flows in the direction whose magnetic effect opposes the change in flux that produced it. This opposition is the meaning of the negative sign in [[Faraday's Law]]. A reinforcing response would create energy without input, so the law is a consequence of energy conservation.

9165.heading: Lens Flare Consistency
9165.content:
Lens flare consists of bright artifacts produced when a strong source reflects and scatters within a camera lens. In many cases the flare elements, image center, and projected light source lie on a common line determined by the optical system.

This relationship can constrain whether a visible sun or lamp occupies the position implied by the flare. Cropping, complex lens designs, added effects, or an off-frame source can change what is visible, so flare should corroborate other lighting evidence rather than stand alone.

9168.title: Length Contraction
9168.heading: Length Contraction
9168.content: Length contraction reduces the measured dimension of an object parallel to its motion. If $L_0$ is proper length in the object's rest frame, an observer seeing it move at speed $v$ measures $L=L_0/\gamma$. The comparison requires simultaneous endpoint measurements in the observer's frame, linking contraction to the relativity of simultaneity.

9171.title: Leibniz Notation
9171.heading: Leibniz Notation
9171.content: Leibniz notation writes the derivative of $y=f(x)$ as $dy/dx$. Although it is not an ordinary fraction, the notation emphasizes the relationship between changes in dependent and independent variables. It makes rules such as the [[Chain Rule]] readable and extends naturally to higher derivatives such as $d^2y/dx^2$.

9174.sourceSearchName: legislative re election strategy legislative re election strategy
9174.title: Legislative Re-Election Strategy
9174.heading: Legislative Re-Election Strategy
9174.content:
A legislative re-election strategy is a pattern of action intended to preserve a lawmaker's political career. Network hypotheses ask whether changing centrality, internal party ties, or cross-group collaboration distinguishes successful candidates.

The examined co-sponsorship case found no simple path shared by re-elected legislators, though combinations of intermediate centrality and homophily appeared in association rules. Exogenous factors remain necessary when the network is only one part of electoral survival.

9175.title: Legislative Re-Election Strategy

9177.title: Legislative Network
9177.heading: Legislative Network
9177.content:
A legislative network represents lawmakers as nodes and a defensible political relationship as an edge. Possible relationships include co-sponsorship, voting similarity, caucus membership, communication, or shared committee work.

The selected edge is a proxy whose institutional validity must be examined. Roll-call, media, and membership ties can be distorted by gatekeeping, selection, or unequal data access, so the network must match the research question.

9179.sourceSearchName: legislative network centrality legislative network centrality
9179.title: Legislative Network Centrality
9179.heading: Document

9180.sourceSearchName: legislative network centrality legislative network centrality
9180.title: Legislative Network Centrality
9180.heading: Legislative Network Centrality
9180.content:
Legislative network centrality measures a lawmaker's relative position in a political graph. Degree counts direct ties, closeness reflects distance to others, and betweenness reflects participation in paths connecting other legislators.

Computing these measures by session reveals how position changes through a term. Centrality alone omits attributes and does not guarantee electoral success, so it can be combined with homophily and other institutional evidence.

9181.sourceSearchName: legislative network centrality legislative network centrality
9181.title: Legislative Network Centrality
9181.heading: References

9183.title: Legislative Homophily
9183.heading: Legislative Homophily
9183.content:
Legislative homophily is the tendency for lawmakers with shared attributes to form political ties. Similar ideology, party, geographic origin, seniority, or prior collaboration can increase the likelihood of co-sponsorship.

Homophily helps explain network cohesion but does not prove why a particular tie formed. Comparing internal and external links can show whether observed collaboration remains mostly inside an attributed group.

9186.title: Legal Positivism
9186.heading: Legal Positivism
9186.content:
Legal positivism explains law through social rules and institutional practices rather than making legal validity depend directly on moral merit. A legal order identifies which norms count as law through criteria accepted and used by its officials.

The framework permits a distinction between what the law is and whether it is morally justified. That separation makes it possible to ask whether privacy is merely enacted protection or an [[Intrinsic Limit of Law]] needed for a viable legal order.

9189.sourceSearchName: legislative co sponsorship legislative co sponsorship
9189.title: Legislative Co-Sponsorship
9189.heading: Legislative Co-Sponsorship
9189.content:
Legislative co-sponsorship is a lawmaker's public support for another legislator's proposal. Repeated acts create ties that can reflect ideology, shared origin, committee collaboration, seniority, social identity, or strategic alliance.

Because the action is recorded with a bill, date, and participants, it supports longitudinal network analysis. Its interpretation still depends on the rules that govern which proposals can be introduced and supported.

9192.title: Left- and Right-Eye Image Separation
9192.heading: Left- and Right-Eye Image Separation
9192.content: Stereoscopic imagery begins with two slightly different horizontal viewpoints of the same scene. The left view must reach the left eye and the right view the right eye; if both eyes receive an identical image, the intended binocular depth is absent. The separation can be provided by a physical barrier, color filters, or another display method. The principle remains the same despite the different devices used to present the views. The offset produces the [[Stereo Parallax and Convergence]] relationship that the viewer interprets as depth.

9195.title: Least Squares Plane
9195.heading: Least Squares Plane
9195.content:
A least squares plane fits observations $(x_i,y_i,z_i)$ with a model such as $z=a+bx+cy$. Its coefficients minimize the sum of squared vertical residuals.

Placing columns of ones, $x$ values, and $y$ values into a matrix turns the problem into [[Linear Least Squares]], so the same normal-equation or factorization methods apply.

9198.title: Left Coset
9198.heading: Left Coset
9198.content:
For a subgroup H of G, the left coset aH contains all products ah with h in H. Two left cosets are either equal or disjoint.

The left cosets partition G, and their number is the index [G:H].

9201.title: Least Squares Approximation
9201.heading: Least Squares Approximation
9201.content:
Least squares approximation chooses model parameters that minimize the sum of squared residuals between observed values and model predictions.

Unlike [[Interpolation]], the fitted function need not pass through every data point. This makes the method suitable for experimental observations containing error and for [[Overdetermined Linear System|overdetermined systems]] with no exact solution.

9204.title: Ledger-Style Database
9204.heading: Ledger-Style Database
9204.content: A ledger-style database records each transaction as a separate row and derives a current balance by aggregating those rows. Inventory additions, sales, and credits remain visible as a history instead of overwriting one quantity field. This gives an audit trail of what changed and can record who made the change, but a growing ledger may need a maintained summary for fast current-state queries.

9207.title: Least Common Mechanism
9207.heading: Least Common Mechanism
9207.content:
The least common mechanism principle minimizes state and mechanisms shared among users or processes. A shared component can become a channel through which one participant corrupts, observes, or interferes with another.

Isolation reduces unintended coupling and simplifies reasoning about failures. Some sharing is necessary, but each common mechanism should have an explicit purpose and strong mediation.

9210.sourceSearchName: least common denominator least common denominator
9210.title: Least Common Denominator
9210.heading: Least Common Denominator
9210.content:
The least common denominator is the smallest positive [[Common Denominator]] for a group of fractions. It is the least common multiple of their denominators.

Using the least common denominator minimizes the size of intermediate numerators and often reduces later simplification. It is convenient rather than mandatory: a larger common multiple still gives a correct sum or difference when every fraction is scaled consistently. For denominators (5) and (7), the least common denominator is (35), although (70), (105), and other common multiples also work.

9213.title: Learning Rate
9213.heading: Learning Rate
9213.content:
The learning rate scales how far a training rule changes model weights in response to an error or gradient. With [[Gradient Descent]], a large rate takes bigger steps through [[Model Weight Space|weight space]]; a small rate takes smaller ones.

Kelleher explains the tradeoff using a ball rolling toward a hole: steps that are too large may pass a useful minimum or make training unstable, while very small steps can make progress slow. The rate is a [[Hyperparameter]] chosen for the training process, not a connection weight learned by the ordinary weight-update rule. Some schedules start larger and reduce it as training progresses.

9216.title: Learn-One-Rule Procedure
9216.heading: Learn-One-Rule Procedure
9216.content:
A learn-one-rule procedure constructs a single antecedent by adding conditions that improve the quality of the examples it covers. Candidate refinements are evaluated until no acceptable gain remains or a stopping condition is met.

The learned consequent names the class favored within the covered region. Repeating the procedure after changing the active training set turns this local search into a complete rule-induction algorithm.
